client: I've been really stressed out lately because of my business finances — I got this unexpected tax bill last week and it completely blindsided me. I'm already stretched thin trying to keep the business afloat, and now this just feels like another weight piling on top of everything. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the bill is still going to be there when I leave this office.
therapist: It makes complete sense that you're feeling overwhelmed — an unexpected financial hit on top of already managing a stretched business is genuinely a lot to carry. You're right that talking won't make the bill disappear, but what we can work on is how your thoughts about this situation might be adding extra weight beyond what's already there, which can actually open up space for clearer problem-solving. What's the thought that feels most heavy or stuck when you imagine dealing with this bill?

client: Honestly, the thought that keeps circling back is that I should have seen this coming — like, a good business owner would have had savings set aside for exactly this kind of thing, and I didn't. It just feels like proof that I'm in over my head and maybe I was never cut out for this in the first place. That thought is the one that won't let me sleep at night.
therapist: That thought — "I was never cut out for this" — is doing a lot of damage quietly, like a slow leak, and it's worth examining whether it's actually true or whether it's a harsh conclusion drawn from one difficult moment. In CBT we'd call this kind of thinking an overgeneralization, where a single setback becomes "proof" of a much bigger, permanent flaw — but missing one tax provision doesn't erase everything you've built or navigated to keep this business running. What would you say to a close friend who came to you with that same thought after hitting an unexpected financial snag?

client: I hear what you're saying, and I know logically that I'd probably tell a friend something like "one mistake doesn't define you" or whatever. But when it's me, it just feels completely different, like the rules don't apply the same way. I've been running this business for six years and somehow this tax thing feels like it cancels all of that out, and I can't just think my way out of that feeling.
therapist: You've just named something really important — that you *know* the kinder perspective logically, but it doesn't land emotionally, and that gap is genuinely frustrating rather than a sign that therapy "won't work" for you. That disconnect between head and heart is incredibly common, and it actually makes sense that six years of effort can feel overshadowed right now, because our minds tend to grab onto threats much more tightly than achievements. I'm curious — when you think about those six years, what's one moment or decision that, even now, you can recognize as something only someone capable would have pulled off?

client: I sit with that question for a moment, because honestly my first instinct is to deflect or say "I don't know." But there was this one time, maybe three years in, where the project I was leading was completely falling apart and everyone else was ready to walk away, and I stayed up for two nights straight restructuring the whole thing and somehow pulled it back from the edge. I can acknowledge that happened, but even saying it out loud right now, there's this voice in the back of my head immediately going "yeah, but that was just luck, or you only did it because you were terrified of failing."
therapist: That story is genuinely remarkable — two nights, a collapsing project, everyone else ready to quit, and you found a way through — and I notice you were able to sit with it for a moment before that dismissive voice rushed in to take it away. That voice saying "it was just luck or fear" is worth looking at closely, because luck doesn't restructure a failing project, and fear alone doesn't either — those take skill and judgment. What do you think it would mean for your sense of yourself as a business owner if you allowed that memory to count as real evidence of capability, rather than an exception to be explained away?

client: I mean... if I actually let myself believe it was real capability and not just some fluke, I think it would feel terrifying, honestly. Because then I'd have to own the expectation that I could do it again, and what if next time I can't? Right now telling myself it was luck feels safer, like it protects me from the pressure of having to live up to something.
therapist: What you've just uncovered is really significant — the "it was luck" story isn't actually about the past, it's a shield you're using to protect yourself from future disappointment, which makes a lot of sense as a strategy even if it comes at a real cost. The tricky thing is that shield also keeps you from accessing your own confidence when you need it most, like right now with this tax situation. I'm wondering — what feels more frightening to you: the possibility of trying and falling short, or going through challenges like this one without ever really trusting yourself?

client: That question kind of stopped me in my tracks, honestly. I think... going through things without trusting myself is scarier, but admitting that feels really uncomfortable because it means I've been making things harder for myself all along. Like, if the "luck" story was just a shield, then I've been choosing to feel small, and I don't know how to sit with that.
therapist: The fact that you're sitting with that discomfort right now, rather than deflecting, is actually courage in action — and it's worth naming that. Realizing you've been carrying an unnecessary weight isn't something to judge yourself for; it's something most people never even get close to seeing clearly about themselves. What do you think it might feel like, even just in small moments, to experiment with letting your own capability be real?

client: I appreciate you saying that, but honestly, even hearing the word "experiment" makes me nervous, like I'm setting myself up to fail again. Because what if I let myself believe I'm capable, and then I mess something up at work, and it just confirms what I've always feared deep down? It feels safer to stay small than to risk that kind of disappointment.
therapist: There's a quiet but real fear underneath what you're describing — not of failure itself, but of what failure would *mean*, as if one mistake would finally confirm the worst thing you believe about yourself. But here's something worth sitting with: you've already messed things up before — the tax bill, the project that nearly fell apart — and you're still here, still running a business, still fighting for it. What if the evidence you're most afraid of already exists, and it didn't actually destroy you?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to agree with it, but it's not that simple. Yeah, I survived those things, but I think I just got lucky, and the next time might be the one that finally proves I really don't know what I'm doing. It's like the fact that I made it through doesn't feel like evidence that I'm capable — it just feels like borrowed time.
therapist: There's something almost exhausting about living on "borrowed time" — never quite letting yourself land, always waiting for the moment everything unravels, and it makes sense that you've settled into a kind of quiet resignation rather than relief after getting through hard things. What I'm noticing is that no amount of evidence seems to be able to break through — the project rescue was luck, surviving the tax bill will be luck — which tells me the belief "I'm not capable" isn't really looking for evidence at all, it's working hard to protect itself. I'm curious — where do you think that belief first took root, because it sounds like it's been with you much longer than this business has?

client: That question kind of stopped me for a second, because I don't usually let myself go back there. I think it started with my dad, honestly — he had this way of pointing out every mistake I made when I was a kid, not cruelly, just very matter-of-factly, like he was cataloguing my failures for future reference. And I guess somewhere along the way I just... took over that job for him.
therapist: What you just said — "I took over that job for him" — is one of the most honest and insightful things a person can say about themselves, and it clearly took something to let yourself go there. That internal critic cataloguing your failures isn't really *you*, it's a voice you inherited and then kept alive long after your dad stopped speaking it, because at some point it felt like the responsible thing to do. I'm wondering — now that you can see where it came from, does it feel any different to hear that critic's voice, knowing it belonged to someone else first?

client: I mean... yeah, it does feel a little different hearing it put that way, like it's not some fundamental truth about me but something I just kind of absorbed. But I'm not sure I can just flip a switch and stop believing it, you know? It's been in my head for so long that it feels like mine even if it wasn't originally.
therapist: You're absolutely right that this doesn't change overnight — a belief that's been living in you for decades isn't going to dissolve in a single conversation, and it would actually be unfair to expect that of yourself. But there's something quietly significant happening here: you've just created a tiny bit of distance between *you* and *the voice*, and that distance, however small, is where change actually begins. What might it look like to start noticing that critic when it shows up, not to silence it, but just to remind yourself where it came from?
